Research Proposal: Confidence-Gated Iterative Pseudo-Labeling with
Phoneme-Constrained Augmentation for Low-Resource ASRTitle: Semi-Supervised
Self-Training with Audited Pseudo-Labels and Phoneme-Preserving Augmentation for
Under-10-Hour Speech Recognition---

Problem
State-of-the-art ASR systems (e.g., Whisper, wav2vec2.0) degrade
catastrophically when fine-tuned on fewer than10 hours of transcribed speech.
Two failure modes dominate: (1) overfitting to the small labeled set, and (2)
confirmation bias in self-training, where the model reinforces its own errors
through noisy pseudo-labels on unlabeled data. No existing method jointly
addresses label quality and data diversity in the under-10-hour regime on a
single pipeline.

Hypothesis
A self-training loop that audits pseudo-labels through a separate
confidence calibrator (rather than the ASR model's own softmax) and couples them
with phoneme-preserving augmentations (time-stretch, pitch-shift, and speed
perturbation clipped to per-phoneme duration bounds) will outperform standard
pseudo-labeling and unsupervised pre-training when labeled data ≤10 hours. The
key claim: auditing prevents confirmation bias, and phoneme-constrained
augmentation prevents the augmentations from destroying linguistic content that
the small labeled set cannot recover.

Method1. Seed model — Fine-tune a small SSL encoder (wav2vec2.0 Base, ~95M
params) on the labeled set (≤10 h). Use a single linear projection head.

2 Pseudo-labeling loop (3 rounds):

• Decode the unlabeled pool with the current model (CTC greedy decoding).
• Audit each pseudo-label: pass the logits to a separate lightweight confidence
estimator (a2-layer MLP over mean-pooled encoder features, trained on the
seed set's held-out fold) and retain only utterances where estimated
confidence ≥0.9 threshold.
• Combine audited pseudo-labeled utterances with the original labeled set.

3 Phoneme-constrained augmentation — Before each training epoch, apply:

• Time stretching (0.85x–1.15x) with per-phoneme duration floor.
• Pitch shift (±2 semitones).
• Speed perturbation (0.9x–1.1x).
• Constraint: a forced-alignment phoneme recognizer (pretrained multilingual)
verifies that the augmented audio's phoneme sequence matches the original;
discard any augmentation where >20% of phonemes shift.

4 Re-train the SSL encoder + projection head from the seed checkpoint on the
combined (labeled + audited pseudo-labeled + augmented) data. Repeat for3
rounds.

Dataset / Benchmark- Primary: Common Voice (Tamil, Sinhala, Catalan, Kyrgyz —4
languages with2–8 h of validated train data each). Evaluate on each language's
official dev/test splits.

• Secondary (sanity check): FLEURS10-hour subset for2 additional languages
(Swahili, Bengali).

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | Purpose |

|---|---| | Character Error Rate (CER) | Primary metric; report mean ± std over3
seeds. | | Word Error Rate (WER) | Secondary, for languages with space-delimited
orthography. | | Pseudo-label acceptance rate | Diagnostic: % unlabeled
utterances retained per round. | | Oracle accuracy of accepted pseudo-labels |
Diagnostic: if a held-out reference exists for the unlabeled pool, measure what
fraction of accepted labels are correct. |

Report effect sizes with95% bootstrap confidence intervals across seeds.

Baselines| Baseline | Why |

|---|---| | Seed-only (fine-tune on labeled data only, no self-training) | Lower
bound — isolates the value of unlabeled data. | | Standard pseudo-labeling (no
auditing, no augmentation) | Ablates the audit mechanism. | | No-augmentation
self-training (audit + pseudo-label, no phoneme constraint) | Ablates the
augmentation contribution. | | SpecAugment self-training (SpecAugment instead of
phoneme-constrained augmentation) | Compares against a widely-used augmentation
baseline. | | wav2vec2.0 Base fine-tuned on full Common Voice (where available,
e.g., Catalan ~80 h) | Upper bound — what performance looks like with abundant
data. | | Whisper Small zero-shot | Compares against a strong multitask model
that has never seen the target language during adaptation. |

Ablations1. Audit threshold sweep — Vary the confidence threshold
(0.7,0.8,0.9,0.95) on one language to measure the precision-recall trade-off in
pseudo-label acceptance.

2 Augmentation constraint strength — Compare the phoneme-preserving constraint
against an unconstrained version (same augmentations, no phoneme-validity
check).
3 Number of self-training rounds — Compare1,2,3, and5 rounds on one language to
measure when performance plateaus or degrades.
4 Size of labeled seed — Sub-sample to1 h,2 h,5 h on a language with8 h
available, and measure whether the method's advantage grows as labeled data
shrinks.

Expected Failure Modes1. Phoneme-constraint too aggressive — The multilingual
forced-aligner may have poor accuracy on a target language it was not trained
on, causing most augmentations to be discarded. Mitigation: Relax the threshold
to40% phoneme shift tolerance; also measure the discard rate and report it.

2 Confidence estimator is poorly calibrated — On languages far from the seed
set, the auditor may either accept noisy labels (false positive) or reject
correct ones (false negative). Mitigation: Use temperature scaling (Platt
scaling) on the confidence estimator; report calibration curves (ECE) per
round.
3 Diminishing returns by round3 — The model may saturate because the unlabeled
pool's acoustic diversity is exhausted. Mitigation: If WER improvement from
round2→3 is <0.5% relative, stop early and report the saturating round as a
finding.
4 CTC beam search decoding with a weak language model — Without a
target-language n-gram or neural LM, decoding may be brittle. Mitigation: Do
not use an external LM for the main experiment (to keep the ablation clean),
but add a shallow fusion with a3-gram LM as a secondary ablation to measure
the orthogonal gain.
5 Hardware constraints — Self-training with augmentation on the full unlabeled
pool (typically50–200 h per language) may be slow. Mitigation: Downsample the
unlabeled pool to20 h per language via random sampling, stratified by speaker
if speaker metadata is available.

**1. Title**
Cross-Lingual Adapter Tuning on Discrete Phonetic Units for Ultra-Low-Resource ASR.

**2. Problem and Motivation**
Fine-tuning massive self-supervised learning (SSL) models like XLS-R or Wav2Vec 2.0 on extremely low-resource languages (e.g., <5 hours of audio) typically leads to catastrophic forgetting of the pre-trained acoustic manifold or severe overfitting. Standard fine-tuning updates millions of parameters, which is unstable with sparse gradients. There is a need for a parameter-efficient approach that leverages discrete acoustic representations to bridge the gap between continuous audio and text in data-starved scenarios.

**3. Core Hypothesis**
Integrating bottleneck adapters into a frozen multilingual SSL backbone, while utilizing discrete k-means units as intermediate targets, will yield lower Word Error Rates (WER) than standard full-parameter fine-tuning by constraining the search space and preserving pre-trained phonetic priors.

**4. Method**
*   **Backbone:** Use a frozen XLS-R (300M or 1B parameter) model as the feature extractor.
*   **Discretization:** Apply a k-means quantizer (trained on the 6th or 9th layer of the SSL model) to convert continuous latent representations into a sequence of discrete "pseudo-units."
*   **Adapter Modules:** Insert lightweight residual bottleneck adapters (rank $r=64$ or $128$) between the Transformer blocks of the encoder. Only the adapters and the final Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC) projection layer are trainable.
*   **Joint Objective:** Train using a hybrid CTC/Attention loss where the encoder is conditioned on discrete units to stabilize the alignment process before mapping to the target character/phoneme set.

**5. Dataset or Benchmark**
*   **Common Voice (v11.0):** Focus on languages with <10 hours of validated data (e.g., Swahili, Kyrgyz, Tatar, or Guarani).
*   **BABEL Development Sets:** Specifically the 1-hour and 10-hour training subsets for low-resource African and Asian languages (e.g., Zulu, Lao).

**6. Evaluation Metrics**
*   **Word Error Rate (WER):** Primary metric for transcription accuracy.
*   **Character Error Rate (CER):** To assess performance on morphologically rich or agglutinative languages.
*   **Parameter Efficiency:** Ratio of trainable parameters to total model size.

**7. Baselines**
*   **Full Fine-Tuning:** Standard XLS-R fine-tuning on the target language.
*   **Wav2Vec 2.0 + CTC:** The original Facebook AI Research (FAIR) implementation for low-resource settings.
*   **ESPnet-Transformer:** A standard E2E Transformer trained from scratch (to demonstrate the necessity of SSL).

**8. Ablations**
*   **Frozen vs. Trainable Backbone:** Testing the impact of freezing the SSL layers.
*   **Discrete vs. Continuous:** Comparing performance when using k-means units as an intermediate step versus direct audio-to-text mapping.
*   **Adapter Position:** Inserting adapters only in the upper layers versus all layers.

**9. Failure Modes and Feasibility Risks**
*   **Unit Mismatch:** Discrete units derived from a multilingual model may fail to capture unique phonemes in outlier languages (e.g., clicks or specific tonal variations).
*   **Capacity Bottleneck:** If the adapter rank is too low, the model may lack the expressivity to learn the mapping from pseudo-units to the target orthography.
*   **Computational Cost:** While parameter-efficient, the inference still requires a full pass through the large frozen backbone, which may be slow on consumer-grade hardware.

There is a need for a parameter-efficient approach that leverages discrete acoustic representations to bridge the gap between continuous audio and text in data-starved scenarios.

**3. Core Hypothesis**
Integrating bottleneck adapters into a frozen multilingual SSL backbone, while utilizing discrete k-means units as intermediate targets, will yield lower Word Error Rates (WER) than standard full-parameter fine-tuning by constraining the search space and preserving pre-trained phonetic priors.

*   **Discretization:** Apply a k-means quantizer (trained on the 6th or 9th layer of the SSL model) to convert continuous latent representations into a sequence of discrete "pseudo-units."
*   **Adapter Modules:** Insert lightweight residual bottleneck adapters (rank $r=64$ or $128$) between the Transformer blocks of the encoder. Only the adapters and the final Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC) projection layer are trainable.

*   **BABEL Development Sets:** Specifically the 1-hour and 10-hour training subsets for low-resource African and Asian languages (e.g., Zulu, Lao).

*   **Word Error Rate (WER):** Primary metric for transcription accuracy.
*   **Character Error Rate (CER):** To assess performance on morphologically rich or agglutinative languages.
*   **Parameter Efficiency:** Ratio of trainable parameters to total model size.

*   **Wav2Vec 2.0 + CTC:** The original Facebook AI Research (FAIR) implementation for low-resource settings.
*   **ESPnet-Transformer:** A standard E2E Transformer trained from scratch (to demonstrate the necessity of SSL).

*   **Frozen vs. Trainable Backbone:** Testing the impact of freezing the SSL layers.
*   **Discrete vs. Continuous:** Comparing performance when using k-means units as an intermediate step versus direct audio-to-text mapping.

*   **Unit Mismatch:** Discrete units derived from a multilingual model may fail to capture unique phonemes in outlier languages (e.g., clicks or specific tonal variations).

Research Proposal: Confidence-Gated Iterative Pseudo-Labeling with
Phoneme-Constrained Augmentation for Low-Resource ASRTitle: Semi-Supervised
Self-Training with Audited Pseudo-Labels and Phoneme-Preserving Augmentation for
Under-10-Hour Speech Recognition---

Problem
State-of-the-art ASR systems (e.g., Whisper, wav2vec2.0) degrade
catastrophically when fine-tuned on fewer than10 hours of transcribed speech.
Two failure modes dominate: (1) overfitting to the small labeled set, and (2)
confirmation bias in self-training, where the model reinforces its own errors
through noisy pseudo-labels on unlabeled data. No existing method jointly
addresses label quality and data diversity in the under-10-hour regime on a
single pipeline.

Hypothesis
A self-training loop that audits pseudo-labels through a separate
confidence calibrator (rather than the ASR model's own softmax) and couples them
with phoneme-preserving augmentations (time-stretch, pitch-shift, and speed
perturbation clipped to per-phoneme duration bounds) will outperform standard
pseudo-labeling and unsupervised pre-training when labeled data ≤10 hours. The
key claim: auditing prevents confirmation bias, and phoneme-constrained
augmentation prevents the augmentations from destroying linguistic content that
the small labeled set cannot recover.

Method1. Seed model — Fine-tune a small SSL encoder (wav2vec2.0 Base, ~95M
params) on the labeled set (≤10 h). Use a single linear projection head.

2 Pseudo-labeling loop (3 rounds):

• Decode the unlabeled pool with the current model (CTC greedy decoding).
• Audit each pseudo-label: pass the logits to a separate lightweight confidence
estimator (a2-layer MLP over mean-pooled encoder features, trained on the
seed set's held-out fold) and retain only utterances where estimated
confidence ≥0.9 threshold.
• Combine audited pseudo-labeled utterances with the original labeled set.

3 Phoneme-constrained augmentation — Before each training epoch, apply:

• Time stretching (0.85x–1.15x) with per-phoneme duration floor.
• Pitch shift (±2 semitones).
• Speed perturbation (0.9x–1.1x).
• Constraint: a forced-alignment phoneme recognizer (pretrained multilingual)
verifies that the augmented audio's phoneme sequence matches the original;
discard any augmentation where >20% of phonemes shift.

4 Re-train the SSL encoder + projection head from the seed checkpoint on the
combined (labeled + audited pseudo-labeled + augmented) data. Repeat for3
rounds.

Dataset / Benchmark- Primary: Common Voice (Tamil, Sinhala, Catalan, Kyrgyz —4
languages with2–8 h of validated train data each). Evaluate on each language's
official dev/test splits.

• Secondary (sanity check): FLEURS10-hour subset for2 additional languages
(Swahili, Bengali).

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | Purpose |

|---|---| | Character Error Rate (CER) | Primary metric; report mean ± std over3
seeds. | | Word Error Rate (WER) | Secondary, for languages with space-delimited
orthography. | | Pseudo-label acceptance rate | Diagnostic: % unlabeled
utterances retained per round. | | Oracle accuracy of accepted pseudo-labels |
Diagnostic: if a held-out reference exists for the unlabeled pool, measure what
fraction of accepted labels are correct. |

Report effect sizes with95% bootstrap confidence intervals across seeds.

Baselines| Baseline | Why |

|---|---| | Seed-only (fine-tune on labeled data only, no self-training) | Lower
bound — isolates the value of unlabeled data. | | Standard pseudo-labeling (no
auditing, no augmentation) | Ablates the audit mechanism. | | No-augmentation
self-training (audit + pseudo-label, no phoneme constraint) | Ablates the
augmentation contribution. | | SpecAugment self-training (SpecAugment instead of
phoneme-constrained augmentation) | Compares against a widely-used augmentation
baseline. | | wav2vec2.0 Base fine-tuned on full Common Voice (where available,
e.g., Catalan ~80 h) | Upper bound — what performance looks like with abundant
data. | | Whisper Small zero-shot | Compares against a strong multitask model
that has never seen the target language during adaptation. |

Ablations1. Audit threshold sweep — Vary the confidence threshold
(0.7,0.8,0.9,0.95) on one language to measure the precision-recall trade-off in
pseudo-label acceptance.

2 Augmentation constraint strength — Compare the phoneme-preserving constraint
against an unconstrained version (same augmentations, no phoneme-validity
check).
3 Number of self-training rounds — Compare1,2,3, and5 rounds on one language to
measure when performance plateaus or degrades.
4 Size of labeled seed — Sub-sample to1 h,2 h,5 h on a language with8 h
available, and measure whether the method's advantage grows as labeled data
shrinks.

Expected Failure Modes1. Phoneme-constraint too aggressive — The multilingual
forced-aligner may have poor accuracy on a target language it was not trained
on, causing most augmentations to be discarded. Mitigation: Relax the threshold
to40% phoneme shift tolerance; also measure the discard rate and report it.

2 Confidence estimator is poorly calibrated — On languages far from the seed
set, the auditor may either accept noisy labels (false positive) or reject
correct ones (false negative). Mitigation: Use temperature scaling (Platt
scaling) on the confidence estimator; report calibration curves (ECE) per
round.

pool's acoustic diversity is exhausted. Mitigation: If WER improvement from
round2→3 is <0.5% relative, stop early and report the saturating round as a
finding.

target-language n-gram or neural LM, decoding may be brittle. Mitigation: Do
not use an external LM for the main experiment (to keep the ablation clean),
but add a shallow fusion with a3-gram LM as a secondary ablation to measure
the orthogonal gain.

pool (typically50–200 h per language) may be slow. Mitigation: Downsample the
unlabeled pool to20 h per language via random sampling, stratified by speaker
if speaker metadata is available.

Research Proposal: Breaking the Performance Ceiling of Small Language Models via
Targeted Capacity Allocation## Title
Beyond Scaling Alone: Targeted Capacity
Allocation for Breaking the Performance Ceiling of Sub-1B Language Models

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Small language models (<1B parameters) exhibit a well-documented but
poorly understood phenomenon: diminishing returns past a critical data scale,
where additional tokens yield negligible or even negative performance gains on
held-out benchmarks. This "performance ceiling" is typically attributed to
insufficient model capacity, but recent evidence suggests that capacity is not
uniformly the bottleneck — certain capabilities (e.g., factual recall,
long-range reasoning) saturate earlier than others (e.g., syntactic fluency,
in-context pattern matching). The research problem is: Can we identify the
precise structural causes of saturation in small models and design targeted
interventions that reallocate limited capacity to the binding constraints?

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
Primary hypothesis: The performance ceiling in small models is driven
by capacity-competition between world-knowledge memorization and compositional
reasoning pathways, not by a global lack of parameters. When a small model
saturates, additional training data primarily overfits its already-congested
feedforward memory (FFN layers) while the attention-based compositional routing
remains underutilized.

Secondary hypothesis: A structured intervention that decouples these two
functions — compressing factual knowledge into a fixed, non-parametric memory
(retrieval augmentation with a small bottleneck) and freeing FFN parameters for
compositional reasoning — will raise the ceiling by10–20% on reasoning-heavy
benchmarks while matching or exceeding baselines on factual recall.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
The proposal has three stages:

Stage1: Ceiling CharacterizationTrain a350M-parameter decoder-only transformer
on increasing data scales (50M,100M,250M,500M,1B,2B,5B,10B tokens). At each
checkpoint, measure per-capability saturation curves across five categories:
factual recall, syntactic well-formedness, short-range reasoning (2 hops),
long-range reasoning (5+ hops), and in-context learning. Use influence functions
and representation similarity (CKA between hidden states at different data
scales) to identify which layers/modules saturate first and correlate with which
capability.

Stage2: Bottleneck DiagnosisInsert capacity probes — lightweight linear
classifiers at each layer that predict whether a given capability fires — to
identify the specific (layer, module) pairs where representation collision
occurs. The hypothesis is that mid-to-late FFN layers become the bottleneck for
factual recall while lower attention layers saturate for compositional
reasoning.

Stage3: Targeted Capacity AllocationIf the diagnosis confirms the hypothesis,
intervene by:

• Retrieval-Augmented Distillation (RAD): Compress the factual knowledge stored
in FFN layers into a small external memory (a frozen key-value store with ~4K
slots). Shrink the model's FFN hidden dimension by25–40% and retrain from
scratch, relying on retrieval for factual queries and freeing FFN capacity
for reasoning.
• Optional control arm: Compare against a naive "bigger FFN" baseline (same
total parameters, no retrieval) to confirm that how capacity is allocated
matters more than how much.

If the diagnosis contradicts the hypothesis (e.g., attention is the bottleneck),
pivot to attention head pruning + reallocation — removing redundant heads to
increase per-head dimensionality.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark- Training: A deduplicated, controlled-quality mix of C4
(natural language), MathPile (math/reasoning), and a synthetic factual QA
dataset (Wiki-QA, ~2M question-answer pairs with provenance). All tokenized with
the same tokenizer to avoid confounds.

• Evaluation (4 benchmarks):
• Factual recall: NaturalQuestions, TriviaQA (exact match)
• Short reasoning: BigBench-Hard subset (boolean expressions, causal judgment)
• Long reasoning: GSM8K (grade-school math, multi-step), HotpotQA (multi-hop
retrieval)
• In-context learning: MMLU (5-shot)
• Saturation diagnosis: Custom probe tasks —500 hand-written examples per
capability with controlled difficulty levels.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | Rationale |

|--------|-----------| | Accuracy (per benchmark) | Primary capability-level
metric | | Saturation threshold (η) | The data scale (in tokens) at which
performance plateaus within1% of final value | | Representation Collapse Score
(RCS) | Average pairwise CKA similarity >0.95 between adjacent data-scale
checkpoints in bottleneck layers — a proxy for when representations stop
differentiating | | Parameter-Utilization Efficiency (PUE) | Per-point
improvement per million train tokens normalized by model size; captures
diminishing returns | | Retrieval Hit Rate (RAD variant only) | Fraction of
queries where the external memory returns the correct factual document |

Primary success signal: RAD variant achieves >10% relative improvement on GSM8K
and HotpotQA over the350M baseline at the same total parameter budget, without
regressing more than2% on NaturalQuestions.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines1. Standard350M decoder (no intervention) — the ceiling-establishing
baseline2. 350M with increased FFN dimension (+25% FFN, -25% attention heads,
same total params) — tests whether naive capacity reallocation achieves similar
gains3. 350M with vanilla RAG (retrieval + standard model, no capacity
reduction) — tests whether retrieval helps regardless of capacity rebalancing4.
Distilled350M from a7B teacher (knowledge distillation alone) — tests whether
the ceiling is a training limitation vs. architectural5. 550M standard decoder
(more parameters entirely) — the "just scale up" ceiling comparison---

Ablations1. RAD without FFN shrinkage — does retrieval help when FFN capacity is
not freed?

2 RAD with different memory sizes (2K,4K,8K slots) — sensitivity to memory
bottleneck3. RAD applied at different layers (early vs. mid vs. late FFN) —
where is compressed storage most effective?
3 Retrieval-free control — train the shrunken-FFN model without retrieval;
isolates whether the gain comes from the architecture change or the
retrieval5. Ceiling characterization on a different architecture (e.g., a350M
MoE with same total params) — is the ceiling mechanism architecture-specific?

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Expected Failure Modes| Failure Mode | Mitigation / Response |

|---|---| | No clear bottleneck emerges (all modules saturate simultaneously) |
The pluralistic-ceiling hypothesis fails. Fallback: test if training recipe (LR
schedule, weight decay) is the real ceiling — ablate optimizer settings. | | RAD
improves reasoning but kills factual recall >2% | Memory size was too small.
Re-run with16K slots or use a learned gating mechanism to route queries. | |
Naive FFN-increase baseline matches or beats RAD | Capacity allocation is not
the bottleneck; the ceiling is truly total-parameter-limited. Concede and report
the negative result as a contribution (important for the community). | | No
ceiling observed (performance continues scaling linearly at10B tokens) | The350M
model was too large for the data scales tested. Scale up to50B tokens or test
a100M model to find the ceiling. | | RAD improves only on seen-document queries
(memorization, not generalization) | Evaluate on held-out timestamps and topics.
If gains vanish, the retrieval store is overfitting to the training set.
Introduce a stricter train/test split on documents. | | CKA-based diagnosis is
inconclusive | Supplement with probing classifiers and leave-one-out accuracy
drops to cross-validate which layers matter for each capability. |

**1. Title**
Recursive Latent-Space Distillation (RLSD): Enhancing Small Language Model Reasoning via Hierarchical Teacher-Trace Alignment.

**2. Problem and Motivation**
Small Language Models (SLMs) under 3B parameters consistently hit a performance ceiling in complex reasoning tasks (e.g., MATH, GSM8K) compared to large-scale models (>70B). Current distillation methods primarily focus on output-layer logit matching or simple supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on Teacher-generated Chain-of-Thought (CoT) data. However, SLMs often lack the internal "representational capacity" to mirror the teacher's logical jumps, leading to "hallucinated reasoning" where the model generates a correct format but incorrect logic. The bottleneck is not just the output, but the lack of structured intermediate latent representations that support multi-step inference.

**3. Core Hypothesis**
By aligning the SLM’s intermediate hidden states with a compressed, projection-mapped version of a Teacher model’s attention manifolds during CoT generation, the SLM can learn the *structural dependencies* of reasoning rather than just the surface-level text. This "Latent-Space Distillation" will allow a <2B parameter model to surpass the performance of a 7B model on logic-dense benchmarks.

**4. Method**
*   **Teacher Model:** Use Llama-3-70B-Instruct or GPT-4 (via API) to generate high-quality CoT traces for a reasoning dataset.
*   **Student Model:** Initialize with Phi-3-mini (3.8B) or TinyLlama-1.1B.
*   **Hierarchical Alignment:**
    1.  **Trace Extraction:** Extract hidden states and attention heads from the Teacher at specific "reasoning nodes" (defined by punctuation or logical connectors like "therefore").
    2.  **Projection Layer:** Implement a learnable linear projection layer ($W_p$) that maps the Student’s lower-dimensional hidden states ($h_s$) to the Teacher’s manifold ($h_t$).
    3.  **Loss Function:** Define a multi-objective loss:
        $L = L_{CE} + \alpha L_{MSE}(W_p h_s, h_t) + \beta L_{KLD}(A_s, A_t)$,
        where $L_{CE}$ is standard cross-entropy, $L_{MSE}$ is the latent alignment loss, and $L_{KLD}$ is the Kullback–Leibler divergence between Student ($A_s$) and Teacher ($A_t$) attention maps.
*   **Recursive Refinement:** Train in two stages: first on general knowledge, then a second pass specifically on the "failure cases" identified by the student during the first pass.

**5. Dataset or Benchmark**
*   **Reasoning:** GSM8K (Grade school math) and MATH (Harder competition math).
*   **Code:** MBPP (Mostly Basic Python Problems).
*   **General:** MMLU (Massive Multitask Language Understanding) to ensure no catastrophic forgetting of general knowledge.

**6. Evaluation Metrics**
*   **Pass@1 Accuracy:** Standard accuracy on reasoning tasks.
*   **Reasoning Fidelity:** A metric measuring the overlap between the Student’s CoT steps and the Teacher’s CoT steps using BLEU/ROUGE on intermediate steps.
*   **Efficiency Ratio:** Performance gain per million parameters compared to the baseline.

**7. Baselines**
*   **Vanilla SFT:** Training the SLM on the same CoT data without latent alignment.
*   **TinyLlama-1.1B / Phi-3-mini:** Base models without specialized distillation.
*   **Knowledge Distillation (KD):** Standard logit-based KD (e.g., using the DistilBERT approach applied to LLMs).

**8. Ablations**
*   **No Latent Alignment:** Removing the $L_{MSE}$ term to test if the projection layer is necessary.
*   **No Attention Matching:** Removing the $L_{KLD}$ term to see if attention structure matters more than hidden state values.
*   **Teacher Scaling:** Using a 7B teacher vs. a 70B teacher to measure the impact of teacher quality on latent mapping.

**9. Failure Modes and Feasibility Risks**
*   **Dimensionality Mismatch:** The gap between a 70B model’s hidden size (e.g., 8192) and an SLM’s (e.g., 2048) may be too wide for a linear projection to capture meaningful nuance, leading to "noise injection."
*   **Overfitting to Teacher Biases:** The student may inherit the specific linguistic quirks or systematic errors of the teacher model.
*   **Computational Cost:** Extracting and storing hidden states for billions of tokens is storage-intensive; this may require "on-the-fly" distillation, which increases training time by 2-3x.

accuracy.

improving selective attention (e.g., structured memory) will help more than
improving planning ability.

**1. Title**
Recursive Latent Knowledge Retrieval (LKR) for Guided Monte Carlo Tree Search in Complex Multi-Hop Reasoning.

**2. Problem and Motivation**
Large Language Models (LLMs) utilizing Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting often suffer from "hallucination cascades," where a single factual error in an intermediate reasoning step invalidates the entire trajectory. While search algorithms like Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) improve reasoning by exploring multiple paths, they typically rely on internal model heuristics for node evaluation. These heuristics are often ungrounded in external facts, leading to "consistent but incorrect" reasoning paths in knowledge-intensive tasks. There is a need for a mechanism that grounds the search process in external evidence at each branching point.

**3. Core Hypothesis**
Integrating a dense retriever into the expansion and evaluation phases of MCTS—where each proposed reasoning step is validated against a retrieved knowledge corpus—will significantly increase the success rate of multi-hop reasoning by pruning branches that contradict external evidence and boosting those with high evidentiary support.

**4. Method**
The system implements a search-based agentic framework:
*   **Expansion (Policy):** Given a state (partial reasoning path), the LLM generates $N$ potential next reasoning steps.
*   **Latent Retrieval:** For each candidate step, a dense retriever (e.g., BGE-M3 or Contriever) queries a vector database (e.g., Wikipedia) to find the top-k relevant passages.
*   **Guided Evaluation (Value Function):** An evaluator LLM receives the candidate step and the retrieved passages. It assigns a scalar reward $R$ based on: (1) Logical consistency with previous steps, and (2) Factual alignment with the retrieved context.
*   **Backpropagation:** The reward $R$ updates the Q-values of the nodes in the MCTS tree.
*   **Termination:** The search continues until a maximum depth is reached or a terminal "Answer" node is generated with high confidence.

**5. Dataset or Benchmark**
*   **StrategyQA:** Requires multi-step implicit reasoning where facts are not explicitly stated in the prompt.
*   **HotpotQA (Distractor Setting):** Requires finding and combining information across multiple documents to answer complex queries.

**6. Evaluation Metrics**
*   **Accuracy:** Pass@1 and Pass@5 (majority vote across multiple MCTS runs).
*   **Reasoning Faithfulness:** The percentage of intermediate steps supported by the retrieved citations (measured via NLI - Natural Language Inference).
*   **Search Efficiency:** The average number of nodes expanded per correct answer.

**7. Baselines**
*   **CoT-SC (Self-Consistency):** Standard Chain-of-Thought with majority voting.
*   **Vanilla MCTS:** Tree search using only the LLM’s internal value judgments without external retrieval.
*   **ReAct:** An agentic baseline that interleaves "Think" and "Act" (Search) steps linearly without tree-based look-ahead.

**8. Ablations**
*   **No-Retrieval MCTS:** To isolate the impact of the search algorithm vs. the knowledge grounding.
*   **Static Retrieval:** Retrieving all documents at the start of the query instead of recursively at each MCTS node.
*   **Random Pruning:** Pruning MCTS branches randomly to ensure the value function (grounded in retrieval) is actually providing signal.

**9. Failure Modes and Feasibility Risks**
*   **Retrieval Latency:** Executing a vector search and an evaluator LLM call for every node expansion is computationally expensive. *Mitigation:* Use small, high-throughput embedding models and cache retrieval results.
*   **Knowledge Noise:** If the retriever returns irrelevant or contradictory snippets, the evaluator may prune correct reasoning paths. *Mitigation:* Implement a "Relevance Filter" that ignores retrieved context if the cosine similarity score is below a specific threshold.
*   **Reward Hacking:** The agent might learn to generate steps that are easy to verify but do not lead to the final answer. *Mitigation:* Weight the final answer's correctness more heavily in the total path reward.

### 1. Title
**Hessian-Guided Channel-Wise Scaling (HGC-Scale): Optimizing 3-bit Integer Quantization for Edge NPU Deployment**

### 2. Problem and Motivation
LLM deployment on edge devices (e.g., mobile SoCs, IoT gateways) is constrained by limited VRAM and the lack of high-throughput floating-point units. While 4-bit Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) is becoming standard, moving to 3-bit or lower often results in a "perplexity cliff" where model utility collapses. This collapse is primarily driven by high-magnitude activation outliers that dominate the quantization scale, crushing the precision of the remaining weights. Existing methods like AWQ or SmoothQuant often rely on per-token scaling or floating-point operations that are inefficient on integer-only Edge Neural Processing Units (NPUs).

### 3. Core Hypothesis
By utilizing a second-order (Hessian-based) sensitivity analysis during a calibration phase, we can identify "salient" weight channels that contribute most to the loss gradient. Applying a static, channel-wise integer scaling factor to these specific channels—rather than uniform scaling—will preserve model accuracy at 3-bit precision while maintaining compatibility with fixed-point NPU arithmetic.

### 4. Method
1.  **Sensitivity Mapping:** Calculate the diagonal of the Hessian matrix for each layer using a small calibration set (e.g., 128 samples from C4) to identify weights with high impact on the output manifold.
2.  **Channel-Wise Re-scaling:** For each weight matrix $W$, introduce a scaling vector $s$ such that $\hat{W} = W \cdot diag(s)$. The values in $s$ are optimized to minimize the reconstruction error $\min ||XW - X\hat{W}||_2$, weighted by the Hessian importance.
3.  **Integer Mapping:** Constrain scaling factors to power-of-two values to allow for bit-shifting operations on edge hardware, avoiding floating-point division during inference.
4.  **Weight Clipping:** Implement an outlier-aware clipping strategy that truncates the top 0.1% of weights based on the Hessian-weighted distribution to maximize the dynamic range of the 3-bit grid.

### 5. Dataset or Benchmark
*   **Calibration:** 128 segments (2048 sequence length) from the **C4 (Colossal Clean Crawled Corpus)** dataset.
*   **Evaluation:**
    *   **Language Modeling:** WikiText-2 and PTB (Perplexity).
    *   **Zero-Shot Tasks:** MMLU (Massive Multitask Language Understanding), HellaSwag, and ARC-Challenge.

### 6. Evaluation Metrics
*   **Accuracy:** Zero-shot task accuracy (%) and Perplexity (PPL).
*   **Efficiency:** Peak Memory Usage (MB), Latency (ms/token) on a target edge device (e.g., Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Gen 2 or Raspberry Pi 5).

Problem
Current LLM-based Text-to-SQL systems perform competitively on benchmarks

question). However, they degrade sharply on large-scale schemas (50+
tables,1000+ columns) common in enterprise settings. Two core issues:

decomposition that scales to schema sizes beyond current benchmarks.

Decomposing the Text-to-SQL task into three sequential stages —
structured schema pruning, sub-query decomposition, and incremental SQL
construction with local verification — will improve execution accuracy on

inference cost.

### 1. Title
**Graph-Pruned Schema Selection (GPSS): Enhancing Text-to-SQL on Large-Scale Databases via Minimal Subgraph Extraction.**

### 2. Problem and Motivation
Current Large Language Model (LLM) based Text-to-SQL systems struggle with "schema noise" in large-scale databases (e.g., the BIRD benchmark). When a database contains hundreds of tables and thousands of columns, providing the entire schema in the prompt leads to:
1. **Context Window Saturation:** Exceeding token limits.
2. **Distraction/Hallucination:** The model selects semantically similar but structurally incorrect columns.
3. **Join Failures:** The model fails to identify the necessary "bridge" tables required to link disparate data points.

Existing RAG-based schema retrieval often treats tables as independent documents, ignoring the relational constraints (Foreign Key dependencies) essential for valid SQL.

### 3. Core Hypothesis
By representing a database schema as a directed multigraph and using a cross-encoder to identify a **minimal connected subgraph** (a Steiner Tree variant) relevant to the natural language query, we can improve SQL Execution Accuracy (EX) compared to standard top-k table retrieval.

### 4. Method
1.  **Schema Graph Construction:** Map the database into a graph $G = (V, E)$. Nodes $V$ are tables and columns; edges $E$ represent Primary Key-Foreign Key (PK-FK) relationships and semantic containment.
2.  **Node Scoring:** Use a Cross-Encoder (e.g., `cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2`) to rank all columns and tables against the user query $Q$.
3.  **Subgraph Extraction:** Identify the top-$N$ highest-scoring nodes. To ensure the LLM can generate valid JOINs, apply a **Steiner Tree heuristic** to find the minimal set of intermediate "bridge" tables that connect these top-$N$ nodes.
4.  **Prompt Construction:** Serialize only the DDL (Data Definition Language) of the extracted subgraph and provide 3-shot in-context examples relevant to the identified domain.
5.  **SQL Generation:** Pass the pruned schema and query to a reasoning-heavy LLM (e.g., GPT-4o or Claude 3.5 Sonnet).

### 5. Dataset or Benchmark
*   **BIRD (Big Bench for Large-scale Database Grounded Text-to-SQL):** Specifically for its large schemas and complex join requirements.
*   **Spider:** For cross-domain generalization testing.

### 6. Evaluation Metrics
*   **Execution Accuracy (EX):** Percentage of queries where the predicted SQL returns the same result as the ground truth.
*   **Valid Efficiency Score (VES):** Measures the computational efficiency of the generated SQL.
*   **Schema Recall:** Percentage of ground-truth tables/columns included in the pruned subgraph.

### 7. Baselines
*   **DIN-SQL:** Decomposed In-Context Learning approach.
*   **RESDSQL:** A ranking-enhanced encoder-decoder framework.
*   **C3:** A ChatGPT-based zero-shot baseline using standard prompt engineering.
*   **Top-K RAG:** Standard vector-store retrieval of tables based on cosine similarity.

### 8. Ablations
*   **Connectivity Constraint:** Remove the Steiner Tree/bridge table logic to see if raw top-k scoring suffices.
*   **Granularity:** Compare Table-level pruning vs. Column-level pruning.
*   **Scoring Model:** Compare a Bi-Encoder (fast) vs. a Cross-Encoder (accurate) for node ranking.

### 9. Failure Modes and Feasibility Risks
*   **Over-Pruning:** The Steiner Tree might exclude a table that contains no keywords from the query but is necessary for a complex filter condition.
*   **Graph Complexity:** In extremely denormalized schemas, the number of possible paths between nodes may lead to a combinatorial explosion during subgraph extraction.
*   **Schema Ambiguity:** If the database lacks explicit PK-FK constraints (common in legacy systems), the graph construction will rely on heuristic name-matching, increasing the risk of disconnected components.

**1. Title**
Decomposing Parametric Memory and Procedural Logic via Low-Rank Modular Intervention.

**2. Problem and Motivation**
Current Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit "capability entanglement," where scaling parameters to improve logical reasoning (e.g., symbolic deduction) simultaneously increases the footprint of parametric memory (e.g., factual trivia). This entanglement leads to "Knowledge-Reasoning Conflicts" (KRC), where a model’s internalized factual errors override correct logical chains provided in-context. Decoupling these capabilities is essential for creating "Reasoning-Only" cores that can be specialized for private, externalized datasets without the overhead or interference of general-purpose parametric knowledge.

**3. Core Hypothesis**
Logical reasoning and factual retrieval occupy distinct, identifiable subspaces within the transformer’s latent representations. By applying rank-constrained modular adapters (LoRA) to specific weight matrices identified via gradient-based sensitivity analysis, it is possible to enhance logical consistency while minimizing the influence of the model’s internal factual database.

**4. Method**
*   **Sensitivity Mapping:** Perform a Taylor-series expansion of the loss function across the layers of a base model (e.g., Llama-3-8B) using two distinct datasets: one focusing on multi-step reasoning (GSM8K) and one on factual recall (WikiText-103).
*   **Subspace Identification:** Identify "Logic-Critical" weights (typically located in the Attention projections) and "Memory-Critical" weights (typically in the MLP up-projections).
*   **Modular Training:** Train "Logic-LoRAs" specifically on the Logic-Critical weights using a reasoning-only corpus.
*   **Decoupling Intervention:** Implement a "Counterfactual Inference" protocol where the model is prompted with premises that contradict its internal training data (e.g., "The capital of France is Tokyo"). A decoupled model should successfully reason from the new premise without reverting to its internal memory.

Large Language Models produce coherent but factually inconsistent outputs

misattribute facts, or assert claims unsupported by their training distribution.
Existing mitigation strategies fall into two camps: (1) inference-time methods
(RAG, self-consistency, contrastive decoding) that add latency and complexity at
deployment, and (2) training-time methods (RLHF, DPO) that rely on expensive
human preference data or simple synthetic negatives that are too easy to
discriminate, leading to weak generalization.

The core gap: training-time objectives lack hard negatives that are semantically
plausible but factually incorrect, produced in a scalable, automated way.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
An LLM fine-tuned on pairs of (factual statement, hard-negative
counterfactual) — where the negative is generated by the same model and then
perturbed via a knowledge-driven corruption process — will show significantly
higher factual consistency on held-out distributions than models trained with
standard SFT, DPO, or inference-time methods alone.

The mechanism is that hard negatives force the model to learn the decision
boundary between factually consistent and inconsistent outputs, rather than
merely memorizing factual-looking surface patterns.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
### Stage1: Hard-Negative Generation PipelineFor each factual triple
(subject, relation, object) extracted from a knowledge base:

1 Prompt the model to generate a natural-language sentence expressing the
triple (e.g., "The Eiffel Tower is located in Paris, France").
2 Generate hard negatives by corrupting the factual triple with four
strategies:

• Entity swap: Replace subject or object with a same-type entity ("The Eiffel
Tower is located in Berlin").
• Relation flip: Replace the relation with a semantically similar but incorrect
one ("The Eiffel Tower was built in Paris" → "The Eiffel Tower was demolished
in Paris" when relation was located_in).
• Numeric/date perturbation: Offset numerical facts by a plausible but wrong
amount ("180 feet" → "280 feet" for height).

creates a contradiction (e.g., substitute a pronoun antecedent).

where the negative is:

• Plausible (the verification model cannot trivially reject)
• Diverse (low semantic similarity to other negatives for the same triple)

• Chosen: Model's own generation of the factual sentence.

The loss encourages higher likelihood of factual trajectories and lower
likelihood of the hard-negative trajectory, using the model's own distribution
as the reference.

query, the model produces K samples; maximize the pairwise agreement of factual

### 1. Title
**Entity-Centric Contrastive Decoding (EC-CD): Mitigating Hallucinations via Knowledge Graph-Constrained Logit Shift**

### 2. Problem and Motivation
Large Language Models (LLMs) frequently exhibit factual inconsistency, particularly "entity swapping" (attributing a correct property to the wrong entity) and "relation fabrication." This occurs because the objective function (next-token prediction) prioritizes local linguistic coherence over global factual constraints. While Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) provides context, the model may still ignore the retrieved evidence in favor of its internal parametric priors. There is a need for an inference-time intervention that forces the model to align its output distribution with verified relational data.

### 3. Core Hypothesis
By contrasting the output logits of a standard LLM with a "fact-aware" distribution derived from retrieved Knowledge Graph (KG) triples, we can suppress tokens that lead to factual drift without requiring expensive fine-tuning or lengthening the prompt context.

### 4. Method
The EC-CD method operates during the decoding phase:
1.  **Entity Extraction:** For a given prompt $Q$, extract key entities using a lightweight NER model (e.g., spaCy).
2.  **KG Retrieval:** Retrieve relevant $(Subject, Relation, Object)$ triples from a structured source (e.g., Wikidata or a domain-specific KG).
3.  **Fact-Aware Logit Bias:**
    *   Define a "Knowledge-Positive" set $S^+$ containing tokens associated with the correct *Object* and *Relation* from the triples.
    *   Define a "Knowledge-Negative" set $S^-$ containing tokens associated with known distractors or high-probability but incorrect entities.
4.  **Contrastive Decoding Formulation:** Modify the logit distribution at each timestep $t$:
    $$L'_{t} = L_{base, t} + \alpha \cdot \mathbb{1}(v \in S^+) - \beta \cdot \mathbb{1}(v \in S^-)$$
    Where $L_{base, t}$ are the original logits, and $\alpha, \beta$ are hyperparameters controlling the strength of the factual constraint.
5.  **Dynamic Adjustment:** Apply the bias only when the model's entropy exceeds a threshold, indicating uncertainty where hallucinations are most likely to occur.

### 5. Dataset or Benchmark
*   **WikiBio Hallucination Benchmark:** For evaluating consistency in biographical summaries.
*   **FEVER (Fact Extraction and VERification):** To test the ability to generate claims that align with provided evidence.
*   **HaluEval:** A large-scale collective of generated and human-annotated hallucinated samples.

### 6. Evaluation Metrics
*   **FactScore:** An automated metric that breaks down generations into atomic facts and verifies them against Wikipedia.
*   **Q^2 (Query-based Question Answering):** Measures the consistency between the generated text and the source via NLI (Natural Language Inference).
*   **Entity Precision/Recall:** Specifically measuring the accuracy of named entity tokens compared to the ground truth triples.
*   **MAUVE:** To ensure that the contrastive decoding does not degrade the overall linguistic quality and human-likeness of the text.

### 7. Baselines
*   **Standard Decoding (Greedy/Top-p):** The base LLM (e.g., Llama-3-8B) without intervention.
*   **RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation):** Providing the KG triples as raw text in the system prompt.
*   **Self-Correction (Chain-of-Verification):** A multi-step prompting approach where the model critiques its own output.
*   **ITI (Inference-Time Intervention):** Shifting activations in the direction of "truthful" heads.

### 8. Ablations
*   **No Negative Bias:** Removing the $\beta$ term to see if penalizing known falsehoods is as critical as rewarding known truths.
*   **Static vs. Dynamic Thresholding:** Testing whether applying the bias at every token (static) is superior to applying it only during high-uncertainty states (dynamic).
*   **Source Quality:** Using "Noisy" KG triples (randomly sampled) to test the robustness of the system against retrieval errors.

### 9. Failure Modes and Feasibility Risks
*   **Entity Ambiguity:** If the NER system fails to resolve entities (e.g., "Amazon" the river vs. the company), the logit bias may enforce incorrect facts.
*   **Fluency Degradation:** Aggressive logit shifting ($\alpha, \beta$ too high) may lead to ungrammatical sequences or repetitive "looping" on entity names.
*   **Latency:** Real-time KG retrieval and logit modification increase the per-token generation time, potentially making it unsuitable for low-latency applications.
*   **KG Coverage:** The method is constrained by the completeness of the Knowledge Graph; facts not present in the KG will default to the base model's (potentially hallucinated) behavior.

Research Proposal: Synthesizing Failure-to-Repair Trajectories for Improving
Code LLM Reasoning## Title
Trajectory-for-Code: Self-Supervised Synthesis of
Debugging Trajectories for Robust Code Generation

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Current code LLMs are predominantly trained on (instruction,
correct_solution) pairs, either from human sources (e.g., StarCoder data) or
synthetic pipelines (e.g., CodeAlpaca, OSS-Instruct). This outcome-only
supervision has two limitations:

1 Brittle reasoning on hard problems — When the model's first attempt is wrong,
it has no training signal for how to recover. It was never shown buggy
attempts, test failures, or the iterative debugging steps that lead to
correct code.
2 Overconfident generations — Models trained exclusively on correct outputs
lack calibrated uncertainty about when their code is likely wrong, and cannot
self-correct without an external oracle.

Gap: While self-debugging and self-refine methods exist at inference time, no
systematic study has asked whether training on synthesized debugging
trajectories (attempt → test failure → bug analysis → repair → verified fix)
improves a model's code reasoning and self-correction ability at both train and
test time.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
Primary: Fine-tuning a code LLM on self-synthesized debugging
trajectories — sequences where the model sees its own buggy attempt, test
failure signal, natural-language bug explanation, and a corrected solution —
improves pass@1 on held-out reasoning benchmarks by ≥5% over fine-tuning on the
same volume of (instruction, correct_code) synthetic data alone.

Secondary: The same training yields a measurable improvement in self-correction
(ability to improve a generation given test feedback at inference time) without
requiring an external verifier during training.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
### Stage1 — Trajectory Synthesis Pipeline (fully automated, no human

### 1. Title
**Exec-Graph: Execution-Verified Synthesis of Multi-Library Logic via Dependency-Graph Perturbation**

### 2. Problem and Motivation
Current code Large Language Models (LLMs) rely heavily on "The Stack" or similar web-scale repositories, which are dominated by repetitive boilerplate and popular frameworks. Consequently, models struggle with **cross-library reasoning** and **low-resource API usage**. Existing synthesis methods like *Evol-Instruct* or *OSS-Instruct* generate instructions but often produce "hallucinated" code that is syntactically correct but logically flawed. There is a critical need for synthetic data that is both diverse and **execution-verified**, ensuring the model learns functional logic rather than just statistical token patterns.

### 3. Core Hypothesis
Fine-tuning a code LLM on synthetic data generated by perturbing real-world Abstract Syntax Trees (ASTs) and verifying the resulting code via runtime unit tests will improve zero-shot performance on complex, multi-library programming tasks by at least 15% compared to instruction-only synthesis.

### 4. Method
1.  **Seed Extraction:** Sample 10,000 high-quality Python/Rust files from *The Stack v2*. Extract dependency graphs and identify API calls to less common libraries (e.g., specialized scientific computing or obscure CLI tools).
2.  **Graph-to-Requirement Transformation:** Use a teacher model (e.g., GPT-4o) to reverse-engineer a natural language requirement from the code, specifically highlighting the interaction between identified libraries.
3.  **Perturbation & Expansion:** Instruct the teacher model to modify the requirement (e.g., "Change the data source from a local CSV to a streaming S3 bucket") while maintaining the core API constraints.
4.  **Synthesis & Test Generation:** Generate a new code solution and a corresponding set of unit tests (using `pytest` or `unittest`).
5.  **Execution Verification (The Filter):** Run the generated code in a sandboxed Docker environment.
    *   **Success:** If tests pass, add the (Requirement, Code) pair to the training set.
    *   **Failure:** Attempt one round of "Self-Debug" based on the traceback; if it fails again, discard the sample.
6.  **Fine-tuning:** Perform Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (LoRA) on a base model (e.g., CodeLlama-7B or DeepSeek-Coder-Base).

### 5. Dataset or Benchmark
*   **Training Seed:** *The Stack v2* (Python/Rust subsets).
*   **Evaluation Benchmark:**
    *   **HumanEval & MBPP:** For general coding proficiency.
    *   **DS-1000:** For data science-specific library usage.
    *   **CrossCodeEval:** For multi-file/multi-library reasoning.

### 6. Evaluation Metrics
*   **Pass@k (k=1, 10, 100):** Functional correctness on benchmarks.
*   **Library Coverage:** The number of unique, non-standard libraries correctly utilized in the generated outputs.
*   **API Hallucination Rate:** Frequency of the model calling non-existent functions or using incorrect signatures.

### 7. Baselines
*   **Base Models:** DeepSeek-Coder-7B-Base, StarCoder2-7B.
*   **Instruction-Tuned Baselines:** WizardCoder (Evol-Instruct), Magicoder (OSS-Instruct).
*   **Direct SFT:** Fine-tuning on the raw seed data without perturbation or verification.

### 8. Ablations
*   **Verification-Only:** Train on synthetic data without the execution-filtering step to measure the impact of data "noise."
*   **Perturbation-Only:** Train on the reverse-engineered requirements of the original code without modifying the logic.
*   **Teacher Model Scaling:** Compare synthesis quality using GPT-3.5 vs. GPT-4o as the generator.

### 9. Failure Modes and Failure Risks
*   **Environment Setup Overhead:** Automatically configuring environments (installing specific libraries) for 10,000+ different code samples is computationally expensive and may fail for libraries requiring specific hardware (e.g., CUDA).
*   **Triviality Bias:** The teacher model might simplify the "perturbed" requirements to ensure the code passes the tests, leading to a dataset of simple, high-pass-rate code that lacks depth.
*   **Data Contamination:** Risk of the "Seed Extraction" phase inadvertently including snippets already present in the evaluation benchmarks.

Research Proposal: Sensitivity-Guided Dynamic Precision Allocation for LLM
Inference## Title
DyPrec: Sensitivity-Guided Dynamic Precision Allocation for
Latency-Optimized LLM Inference

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
LLM inference latency is dominated by memory bandwidth in the decode
phase — each token generated requires loading the full model weights from GPU
memory. While static quantization (e.g., FP16→FP8/FP4) reduces this cost
uniformly, it applies a single precision floor to all layers regardless of their
actual sensitivity to numerical error. This is wasteful: embedding and early
layers are highly sensitive to quantization drift (errors compound across
depth), while later layers and feed-forward sub-layers can tolerate much lower
precision without measurable output degradation. Current systems lack a
principled method to dynamically allocate precision per layer and per input at
inference time.

Key gap: No existing work jointly optimizes the granularity (per-layer,
per-block) and adaptivity (per-input, per-token position) of precision
allocation using empirical sensitivity measurements, while respecting hardware
constraints (group size, memory alignment, kernel availability).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
Given an LLM and a target accuracy budget (e.g., ≤0.5% degradation in
downstream task accuracy), there exists, for each layer, a minimum viable
precision that respects the sensitivity profile of that layer. Allocating higher
precision only to the most sensitive layers and lower precision to insensitive
ones yields a better latency–accuracy Pareto frontier than any uniform-precision
baseline. Further, this allocation can be dynamically selected per input cluster
(e.g., domain or difficulty) to improve the frontier over a static
one-size-fits-all allocation.

### 1. Title
Adaptive Layer-Skipping for Self-Speculative Decoding (ALS-SSD)

### 2. Problem and Motivation
The primary bottleneck in Large Language Model (LLM) inference is the autoregressive nature of decoding, which is memory-bandwidth bound. While speculative decoding (e.g., using a small drafter model like TinyLlama to assist Llama-3) reduces latency, it introduces the complexity of managing two distinct models and synchronization overhead. Furthermore, fixed drafting strategies do not account for the varying computational complexity of tokens (e.g., "the" vs. "Riemann"). Existing "Medusa-style" heads require significant fine-tuning and additional parameters.

### 3. Core Hypothesis
Early-layer representations in deep Transformer architectures contain sufficient semantic information to predict the final token distribution for high-probability tokens. By implementing a dynamic "exit-and-verify" mechanism within a single model—using early-layer outputs as drafts—we can achieve a 1.5x–2.0x speedup with zero degradation in output quality and minimal memory overhead.

### 4. Method
*   **Layer Exit Selection:** Identify an "exit layer" $L_e$ (typically at $1/4$ or $1/3$ of total depth $L$).
*   **Self-Drafting:** For a given sequence, compute activations up to $L_e$. Use a lightweight, pre-trained linear projection (an "Auxiliary Exit Head") to generate a $k$-token draft sequence.
*   **Dynamic Thresholding:** Implement an entropy-based gate. If the softmax entropy of the exit head's prediction exceeds a threshold $\tau$, the model reverts to standard decoding for that token, as the early-layer representation is deemed insufficient.
*   **Parallel Verification:** Feed the $k$-token draft into the full $L$-layer model. Use a single forward pass with a causal mask modification to verify all $k$ tokens simultaneously, following the standard speculative decoding verification logic (Rejection Sampling).
*   **KV-Cache Management:** Employ a dual-cache pointer system where the draft tokens occupy temporary slots in the PagedAttention blocks until verified.

### 5. Dataset or Benchmark
*   **General:** ShareGPT-v3 (conversational).
*   **Reasoning:** GSM8K (mathematical word problems).
*   **Code:** HumanEval (Python completion).
*   **Long Context:** NarrativeQA (to test KV-cache pressure).

### 6. Evaluation Metrics
*   **Tokens Per Second (TPS):** Throughput measurement.
*   **Speedup Ratio:** $\text{TPS}_{\text{ALS-SSD}} / \text{TPS}_{\text{Autoregressive}}$.
*   **Acceptance Rate ($\alpha$):** The average number of tokens accepted per speculative draft.
*   **Perplexity Parity:** Ensure the output distribution remains mathematically identical to the base model.
*   **Time-to-First-Token (TTFT):** Ensure the exit head does not significantly delay the initial response.

### 7. Baselines
*   **Standard Autoregressive Decoding:** Vanilla Llama-3-8B/70B.
*   **vLLM (PagedAttention):** Current industry standard for high-throughput inference.
*   **Medusa:** Multiple-head speculative decoding (requires fine-tuning).
*   **Lookahead Decoding:** Jacobi-iteration-based parallel decoding without a draft model.

### 8. Ablations
*   **Exit Layer Depth:** Test $L_e$ at $L/8, L/4, L/2$ to find the optimal trade-off between draft accuracy and compute savings.
*   **Threshold $\tau$ Sensitivity:** Vary the entropy threshold to measure the impact of "conservative" vs. "aggressive" drafting.
*   **Exit Head Complexity:** Compare a simple Linear head vs. a 2-layer MLP head.

### 9. Failure Modes and Feasibility Risks
*   **Low Acceptance Rate in Complex Reasoning:** In tasks like GSM8K, early layers may fail to predict complex logical steps, causing the acceptance rate to drop to zero and introducing the overhead of the exit head without gain.
*   **Memory Bandwidth of Exit Head:** If the auxiliary head is too large, the time taken to compute the draft might outweigh the time saved by skipping layers.
*   **KV-Cache Fragmentation:** Frequent "rejection" of draft tokens may lead to fragmentation in PagedAttention, requiring more aggressive garbage collection.

*   **KV-Cache Management:** Employ a dual-cache pointer system where the draft tokens occupy temporary slots in the PagedAttention blocks until verified.

*   **Long Context:** NarrativeQA (to test KV-cache pressure).

*   **Tokens Per Second (TPS):** Throughput measurement.
*   **Speedup Ratio:** $\text{TPS}_{\text{ALS-SSD}} / \text{TPS}_{\text{Autoregressive}}$.
*   **Acceptance Rate ($\alpha$):** The average number of tokens accepted per speculative draft.
*   **Perplexity Parity:** Ensure the output distribution remains mathematically identical to the base model.
*   **Time-to-First-Token (TTFT):** Ensure the exit head does not significantly delay the initial response.

### 7. Baselines
*   **Standard Autoregressive Decoding:** Vanilla Llama-3-8B/70B.
*   **vLLM (PagedAttention):** Current industry standard for high-throughput inference.
*   **Medusa:** Multiple-head speculative decoding (requires fine-tuning).
*   **Lookahead Decoding:** Jacobi-iteration-based parallel decoding without a draft model.

### 8. Ablations
*   **Exit Layer Depth:** Test $L_e$ at $L/8, L/4, L/2$ to find the optimal trade-off between draft accuracy and compute savings.

*   **Exit Head Complexity:** Compare a simple Linear head vs. a 2-layer MLP head.

*   **Low Acceptance Rate in Complex Reasoning:** In tasks like GSM8K, early layers may fail to predict complex logical steps, causing the acceptance rate to drop to zero and introducing the overhead of the exit head without gain.

they disproportionately map neutral-source occupational terms (e.g., "doctor,"
"nurse") to target-language gendered forms that align with statistical
stereotypes rather than real-world distributions. On standard benchmarks like
WinoMT, models such as mBART-50 assign "She is a doctor" the masculine
translation ~85% of the time for English→Spanish, while "nurse" is feminine ~80%
of the time. This propagates occupational stereotypes and can produce
grammatically incorrect output when the context or world knowledge contradicts
the majority pattern.

Existing debiasing approaches fall into three camps — (1) post-hoc decoding
rules, (2) fine-tuning on balanced or anti-stereotypical data, and (3)
embedding-space interventions — but each has limitations: decoding rules can
break fluency, balanced data is scarce and expensive, and embedding
interventions are often task-specific and degrade general translation quality. A
method that requires only synthetic data and a single fine-tuning step, without
specialized architectures or inference-time overhead, would be broadly
applicable across language pairs and model families.

Hypothesis
Adding counterfactually augmented training examples — where
occupational nouns are swapped across genders in the source sentence — combined
with a source-side gender control signal (a special token marking the intended
target gender) will significantly reduce occupational gender bias in NMT output
on WinoMT while preserving BLEU score on standard translation benchmarks
within0.5 points.

that doctor can co-occur with feminine agreement in the target, breaking the
spurious correlation; (b) the control token lets the model disambiguate
ambiguous cases at inference without requiring a separate classifier or post-hoc
rule.

EN→ES/DE/FR).

occupation lexicon (300 occupation nouns from ONET).

descriptor ("the male doctor").

translation obtained by replacing gender-agreement morphology in the
reference.

**1. Title**
Contrastive Latent Alignment for Morphological Gender Consistency in Machine Translation (CLA-MT).

**2. Problem and Motivation**
Neural Machine Translation (NMT) models frequently inherit and amplify sociodemographic biases present in training corpora, such as associating specific occupations with binary genders (e.g., "doctor" as masculine). Current debiasing methods, like Counterfactual Data Augmentation (CDA), often treat tokens in isolation. This fails in morphologically rich languages (e.g., Spanish, Arabic) where gender agreement must propagate across adjectives, determiners, and verbs. Furthermore, aggressive debiasing often leads to "catastrophic forgetting" of general translation quality, reducing BLEU scores.

**3. Core Hypothesis**
A multi-task objective that combines standard cross-entropy loss with a contrastive loss—minimizing the distance between the latent representations of original and gender-swapped counterfactual sentence pairs—will improve gender translation accuracy on professional terms while maintaining parity in general translation quality.

**4. Method**
*   **Data Preparation:** Use a rule-based approach to generate a counterfactual corpus ($D_{cf}$) from a subset of the training data ($D_{orig}$) by swapping gendered terms and applying morphological re-inflection using tools like Spacy or Trankit.
*   **Dual-Objective Training:** Train a Transformer-based NMT model using a combined loss function: $L = L_{NMT} + \lambda L_{CL}$.
    *   $L_{NMT}$: Standard label-smoothed cross-entropy on $D_{orig} \cup D_{cf}$.
    *   $L_{CL}$ (Contrastive Loss): For a pair $(s, s_{cf})$, minimize the cosine distance between the encoder’s mean-pooled hidden states $H_s$ and $H_{s_{cf}}$. This forces the encoder to learn gender-invariant semantic representations for the underlying concepts.
*   **Inference:** Standard beam search decoding; no additional computational overhead at runtime.

**5. Dataset or Benchmark**
*   **Training:** WMT14 English-Spanish (En-Es) and English-French (En-Fr) to test morphological agreement.
*   **Evaluation:**
    *   **WinoMT:** A professional-occupation challenge set for gender bias.
    *   **MuST-SHE:** A benchmark for gender translation in speech-to-text/text-to-text contexts.
    *   **General Quality:** FLORES-201 or WMT test sets.

**6. Evaluation Metrics**
*   **Primary Bias Metric:** Accuracy on WinoMT (specifically the "Pro-stereotypical" vs. "Anti-stereotypical" gap).
*   **Translation Quality:** BLEU, chrF, and COMET scores.
*   **Consistency Metric:** Gender Parity Score (GPS), measuring how often the model produces the same translation quality regardless of the input gender.

**7. Baselines**
*   **Vanilla Transformer-Base:** Standard training on WMT without debiasing.
*   **CDA-Only:** Fine-tuning the Vanilla model on the counterfactual dataset without the contrastive loss.
*   **Null Space Projection (INLP):** A post-hoc debiasing method that removes gender information from the latent space by projecting it onto the null space of a gender classifier.

**8. Ablations**
*   **Effect of $\lambda$:** Vary the weight of the contrastive loss (0.1, 0.5, 1.0) to find the Pareto frontier between debiasing and BLEU.
*   **Encoder vs. Decoder Alignment:** Apply $L_{CL}$ only to the encoder, only to the decoder, or both.
*   **Re-inflection Quality:** Compare results using simple word-swapping vs. full morphological re-inflection to quantify the impact of grammatical consistency in $D_{cf}$.

**9. Failure Modes and Feasibility Risks**
*   **Morphological Noise:** Rule-based re-inflection may introduce grammatical errors in the counterfactual set, potentially teaching the model incorrect syntax.
*   **Semantic Drift:** Forcing $H_s$ and $H_{s_{cf}}$ to be too close may prevent the model from distinguishing gender when it is contextually relevant (e.g., translating a biography).
*   **Resource Constraints:** Contrastive learning on large-scale NMT requires significantly more VRAM due to the need to process pairs of sentences simultaneously. Mitigation: Use a smaller, targeted subset for the contrastive objective.

Research Proposal: Adaptive Knowledge Injection via Confidence-Gated Adapter
Fusion for Domain-Specific LLMs## Title
Confidence-Gated Adapter Fusion for
Mitigating Knowledge Conflicts During Domain-Specific LLM Injection

Problem
Domain-specific LLM deployment (legal, medical, finance) requires
injecting specialized knowledge into general-purpose pre-trained models. Three
interrelated challenges remain unresolved:

1 Knowledge conflicts — injected domain facts contradict or compete with the
model's pre-training knowledge, causing inconsistent behavior depending on
prompt phrasing.
2 Selective forgetting — fine-tuning on domain text degrades general-language
capabilities, especially on reasoning and rare-token recall.
3 Sub-domain interference — a single domain (e.g., clinical medicine) contains
heterogeneous sub-domains (radiology, pathology, pharmacology) that interfere
when injected via a single adapter or fine-tuning run.

Current solutions (full fine-tuning, RAG, LoRA, model editing) each address only
a subset of these. No method jointly handles all three while providing per-input
routing between base and injected knowledge.

Hypothesis
Confidence-gated routing — where the model dynamically selects between
base knowledge and injected domain knowledge based on its own predictive
uncertainty — reduces knowledge conflicts and sub-domain interference compared
to monolithic injection, while preserving general capabilities better than full
fine-tuning and matching the domain accuracy of state-of-the-art fixed injection
methods.

More concretely: an adapter mixture with a learned confidence-gating mechanism
will achieve higher domain-specific accuracy and lower general-task degradation
than the Pareto frontier of existing injection methods.

Method
Architecture. Start with a frozen base LLM (e.g., Llama-3-8B). We train a
set of k lightweight LoRA adapters, each specialized on a distinct sub-domain
cluster of the target domain (clusters discovered via topic modeling or
metadata-driven splits). A small learned confidence gate is trained to produce,
for each input token/sequence: (a) a routing weight over the k adapters, and (b)
a scalar β ∈ [0,1] that mixes the adapter output with the base model's original
hidden state. When β is low, the model relies on base knowledge; when high,
injected knowledge dominates.

Gate architecture. A2-layer MLP over the hidden state of the last layer at the
final token position, outputting a softmax over adapters and a sigmoid-gated β.
Trained jointly with adapters via a regularized objective.

Training objective. Two terms:

• Domain accuracy — standard cross-entropy on domain data, but weighted by a
per-sample confidence bonus that down-weights examples the base model already
answers well (to focus injection on genuinely novel knowledge).
• General capability preservation — a distillation regularizer that penalizes
large β when the base model's output distribution on held-out general
benchmarks (MMLU subsets, GSM8K) has low entropy (high confidence),
preventing unnecessary overrides.

Inference. Single forward pass per token. Gating adds negligible latency (<1%
parameter overhead).

Dataset / Benchmark
We construct a multi-sub-domain biomedical benchmark from
public sources:

Sub-domain           Dataset                            Size         Source

### 1. Title
**Contrastive Knowledge Injection via Structured-Latent Alignment (CKI-SLA)**

### 2. Problem and Motivation
Domain-specific Large Language Models (LLMs) face two primary hurdles: **Knowledge Conflict** (where pre-existing parametric weights contradict new domain-specific facts) and **Catastrophic Forgetting** (where domain tuning degrades general-purpose reasoning). Current methods like Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) suffer from retrieval noise and context window saturation, while standard Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) often fails to anchor model weights to structured factual hierarchies, leading to "hallucinated" domain logic.

### 3. Core Hypothesis
Aligning the LLM’s latent hidden states with structured Knowledge Graph (KG) embeddings via a contrastive objective—specifically targeting the Feed-Forward Network (FFN) layers—will increase factual precision and reduce parametric drift compared to standard token-level cross-entropy training.

### 4. Method
1.  **Entity Mapping:** Extract (Subject, Relation, Object) triples from a domain-specific KG. Map these entities to their corresponding token spans in a domain corpus using an Entity Linker (e.g., REL or Spacy).
2.  **Structured Embedding Projection:** Pre-compute KG embeddings using a translational model (e.g., **RotatE**). Train a linear projection layer ($W_p$) to map these KG embeddings into the LLM’s hidden dimension.
3.  **Contrastive Alignment:** During fine-tuning, implement a dual-objective loss:
    *   **$\mathcal{L}_{CLM}$:** Standard Causal Language Modeling loss.
    *   **$\mathcal{L}_{Align}$:** A InfoNCE contrastive loss that maximizes the similarity between the LLM's hidden state at the entity token position and the projected KG embedding, while minimizing similarity with non-matching entities in the batch.
4.  **PEFT Integration:** Apply the alignment objective only to **LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation)** weights in the MLP/FFN layers, which are hypothesized to store the bulk of factual knowledge.

### 5. Dataset or Benchmark
*   **Knowledge Source:** **UMLS (Unified Medical Language System)** for medical triples.
*   **Training Corpus:** A subset of **PubMed Central (PMC)** open-access papers.
*   **Evaluation:** **MedQA (USMLE)** for multi-choice reasoning and **PubMedQA** for domain-specific question answering.

### 6. Evaluation Metrics
*   **Accuracy / F1-Score:** Standard performance on MedQA.
*   **Knowledge Retention Score (KRS):** Performance delta on the **MMLU (Massive Multitask Language Understanding)** general benchmark to measure catastrophic forgetting.
*   **Faithfulness Rate:** Using NLI-based entailment to check if model outputs are supported by the UMLS source triples.

### 7. Baselines
*   **Base Model:** Llama-3-8B (unmodified).
*   **RAG Baseline:** Llama-3-8B with BM25/Contriever-based retrieval from the PMC corpus.
*   **LoRA-SFT:** Standard fine-tuning on PMC text without the contrastive KG alignment objective.
*   **K-Adapter:** An existing modular knowledge injection framework.

### 8. Ablations
*   **Objective Impact:** Train with $\mathcal{L}_{CLM}$ only vs. $\mathcal{L}_{CLM} + \mathcal{L}_{Align}$.
*   **Layer Targeting:** Apply alignment to Attention layers vs. FFN layers.
*   **Embedding Source:** Use random entity initialization instead of pre-trained RotatE KG embeddings to test the value of structured topology.

### 9. Failure Modes and Feasibility Risks
*   **Entity Disambiguation Errors:** If the entity linker incorrectly maps a token to a KG node, the contrastive objective will inject noise into the latent space.
*   **Latent Space Collapse:** If the contrastive temperature is too low, the model's hidden states may converge to a narrow manifold, destroying linguistic diversity.
*   **Computational Overhead:** Pre-computing KG embeddings for millions of triples in UMLS requires significant memory; mitigation involves using a pruned "Core" subset of the KG.
